title_content.content: Construction of 1,3-Diboryl Allenes from gem-Iododiboron Compounds via Intermolecular Boryl Group Transfer<sup>†</sup>

paragraph_content.content: Ming Li,<sup>a</sup> Yi Wei,<sup>a</sup> Du Chen,<sup>c</sup> Peng-Fei Ning,<sup>a</sup> Yi-Fei Yang,<sup>a</sup> Xiao-Yu Xie,<sup>a</sup> Chao Liu,*<sup>,c</sup> and Kai Hong*<sup>,a,b</sup>

<sup>a</sup> Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Molecular Therapeutics and New Drug Development, School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering, East China Normal University, 3663 N Zhongshan Road, Shanghai 200062, China
<sup>b</sup> Shanghai Frontiers Science Center of Molecule Intelligent Syntheses, School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering,
East China Normal University, 3663 N Zhongshan Road, Shanghai 200062, China
<sup>c</sup> State Key Laboratory for Oxo Synthesis and Selective Oxidation, Lanzhou Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Lanzhou, Gansu 730000, China
Allenes | Organoboron | Iododiboron | Grignard reagents | Isomerization | Migration | Organohalides | Isotopes | Nucleophilic substitution | Synthetic methods

Allenylboronates are valuable synthetic building blocks and have garnered significant interest. However, their 1,3-diboyl substituted analogs have not been reported. Herein, we disclosed a novel method for creating 1,3-diboyl allenes from gem-iododiboron compounds and alkynyl Grignard reagents. The starting materials are initially converted into the corresponding propargylic gem-bis(boronates), which then undergo an intermolecular boryl group transfer to afford 1,3-diboyl allenes, as confirmed by mechanistic studies. This method features good tolerance to steric hindrance and is compatible with a wide variety of functional groups.

paragraph_content.content: Allenes are a unique class of unsaturated compounds with a cumulative double-bond skeleton, having widespread applications in natural product synthesis, pharmaceutical chemistry, and materials science.<sup>[1]</sup> Allenylboron compounds,<sup>[2]</sup> in particular, have proven themselves to be valuable building blocks in propargylation, allenylation,<sup>[3-4]</sup> and many other useful transformations.<sup>[5]</sup> Moreover, the versatile
{ \mathsf { C } } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathsf { B } }

bond can be readily converted into various functional groups.<sup>[6]</sup> Thus, chemists have persisted in seeking methods for the facile synthesis of allenylboronates from readily available starting materials. Currently, the two major approaches are: 1) boryl substitution of propargylic compounds bearing a leaving group<sup>[7]</sup> and 2) hydroboration of enynes with HB(pin) or
H _ { B } ( \mathsf { c a t } ) ^ { [ 8 ] } .

(Scheme 1A). Recently, more strategies, such as olefin metathesis<sup>[9]</sup> and hydrazination/fragmentation of alkynyl boronates,<sup>[10]</sup> have been reported. Intriguingly, allenylboronates can also be accessed from the isomerization of propargylic boron compounds,<sup>[11-12]</sup> featuring an intramolecular boryl group migration as the key step (Scheme 1B). Despite the extensive study of the synthesis and application of allenylboronates, research on diboryl-substituted allenes remains elusive. Given the unique reactivities of the analogous diboryl alkene species,<sup>[13]</sup> the synthetic protocols for diboryl allenes are highly desired.

Halogenated geminal bis(boronates) have recently emerged as versatile synthons and attracted significant attention.<sup>[14]</sup> I ndependent research by Cho,<sup>[15]</sup> Liu,<sup>[16]</sup> a nd Hong<sup>[17]</sup> groups has led to the development of substitution reactions of halogenated gem-diboron compounds with various nucleophiles. While most
\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 } -

and sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridized Grignard reagents were compatible and yielded formal substitution products,<sup>[17]</sup> we discovered that the sp-hybridized Grignard reagents, i.e., alkynyl magnesium halides, produced 1,3-diboryl allenes predominantly (Scheme 1C). In this paper, we present the development of this method and the mechanistic studies behind this unprecedented transformation.

Our investigation commenced with the addition of alkynyl Grignard reagent 2a to an α-halogenated gem-diboron compound 1 (Table 1). According to our previous studies,<sup>[17]</sup> the halogen substituent and the cosolvent were found crucial to the reaction. After initial tests, excellent yield was observed when the gem-diboryl iodide 1c was employed as the substrate (entries 1—3). Due to the lower reactivity of the sp-hybridized carbanion, magnesium-iodine exchange, which was previously observed with aryl and alkyl Grignard reagents, did not occur. To our delight, the propargyl gem-diboron product 3a was not generated, which is otherwise challenging to separate. The addition of toluene as the cosolvent was not necessary compared to pure THF or diethyl ether/THF system (entries 4 and 5). However, with toluene, the reaction was homogeneous, which was preferred for further study. 1,4-Dioxane, DME, and cyclohexane, however, hampered the reaction efficiency and provided 3a as the major product (entries 6—8). Lastly, alkynyl lithium and zinc reagents were investigated, and the desired product was also observed, albeit in lower yield (entries 9 and 10).

paragraph_content.content: With the optimal condition in hand, the scope of Grignard reagents was explored first using 1c as the standard substrate (Table 2A). The diboryl allene skeleton of 4a was confirmed by single crystal X-ray diffraction. A gram-scale experiment was also performed under the standard conditions. The yield slightly diminished due to the prolonged purification on silica gel. This protocol was not sensitive to the steric hindrance on the far side of the alkynyl reagents. Products with both linear chains and hindered quaternary carbon centers were obtained in good yields (4b—4e). Grignard reagents bearing alkenyl (4g) and aryl groups (4h—4p) also performed well. A variety of electron-donating and withdrawing substituents at the ortho-, meta- and para-positions were compatible with little impact on the overall efficiency. Notably, this method was also competent to naphthyl group (4o) and aromatic heterocycles (4f and 4p). Additionally, a corresponding product with geminal silyl and boryl substitution (4q) was obtained in excellent yield, providing potential for chemoselective [7a,18] transformation.

Next, we examined the scope of the iododiboron compounds using a 3-phenyl-1-propyne-derived Grignard reagent (Table 2B). A wide range of linear and branched alkyl substituents with different sizes and functional groups were surveyed. The products were obtained in high yields in most cases (4r—4ag). Notably, the sterically hindered tert-butyl group was well tolerated (4y). Despite the use of gem-diboryl bromide due to the preparation method of the starting material,<sup>[19]</sup> high efficiency was maintained. Functional groups such as bromo and pyridyl groups, acetal, ether, and allyl groups were all compatible. However, the product possessing an ester group was collected in only 45% yield (4af). This inferior result was presumably attributed to the coordination between the carbonyl oxygen and the boron atom, which might facilitate the enolate formation and interfere with the desired reaction. Lastly, the suitability of silyl (4ah) and aryl group (4ai) for this protocol was also confirmed.

paragraph_content.content: Our efforts were then devoted to elucidating the reaction mechanism. Initially, substrate
{ \mathfrak { s } } ,

in which one of the B(pin) groups was replaced with a methyl group, was subjected to the standard condition (Scheme 2A). The reaction efficiency decreased significantly, and more importantly, propargyl boronate 6 emerged as the primary product. This outcome aligned with the results in Table 1 (entries 6—8), suggesting that the reaction may involve a formal substitution followed by an isomerization step, both potentially promoted by the geminal diboryl groups. To further validate this hypothesis, we carried out the reaction using iododiboron 1c
\mathsf { a t } - 3 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathsf C ,

, and isolated the corresponding propargyl gem-diboron compound 8 as the sole product in 52% yield (Scheme 2B). Subsequently, with the addition of a catalytic amount of Grignard reagent, compound 8 underwent complete isomerization to 1,3-diboryl allene 4b in 80% NMR yield (Scheme 2C).

In previous studies by Soderquist and Zhu (Scheme 1B), intramolecular boryl migration was proposed to explain the isomerization.<sup>[11]</sup> To investigate whether our reaction follows a similar mechanism, we conducted an isotope-labeling crossover experiment (Scheme 2D). We initially combined <sup>10</sup>B-labeled

with unlabeled 1d in a 1 : 1 ratio and then exposed the mixture to the standard condition. The resulting products, 4b and 4ae, were isolated and analyzed using high-resolution mass spectroscopy (HRMS). Upon comparing the spectra of the collected product 4b to that of authentic <sup>10</sup>B-4b and unlabeled 4b with natural abundance, it became evident that there was a scrambling of boryl groups between <sup>10</sup>B-1c and 1d. The same phenomenon was also observed for 4ae (for HRMS spectra, see Supporting Information). This outcome strongly indicated that an intermolecular pathway is the predominant, if not the sole, route during the isomerization.

To provide additional mechanistic insights, we performed another isotope-labeling experiment. Specifically, we conducted the isomerization of <sup>10</sup>B-8 in the presence of a stoichiometric amount of unlabeled alkynyl boronate 9 (Scheme 2E). The HRMS spectrum of product <sup>mix</sup>B-4b further confirmed the involvement of an alkynyl boronate species in the major pathway.

paragraph_content.content: In light of the mechanistic experiments and our previous studies,<sup>[17]</sup> a plausible mechanism is proposed in Scheme 2F. Substrate 10 was initially converted into gem-diboryl alkyne 12 through the formation of ate-complex 11, followed by a 1,2-metallate shift. The coordination of compound 12 with excess Grignard reagent generates ate-complex 13, and the cleavage of the C—B bond leads to the formation of a more stable sp -hybridized carbanion 14. This carbanion can serve as a Lewis base to abstract a boryl group from alkynyl boronate 9 to afford the desired product 16. The resulting alkynyl carbanion 15 can then activate another molecule of 12 in a catalytic manner (Path A with red arrows). The alternative pathway involves a boryl transfer from another molecule of 12 through the intermediacy of ate-complex 17, yielding compounds 16 and 14, which can then sustain a chain process (Path B with blue arrows). Based on the current information, the occurrence of Path A can be confirmed. However, both pathways appear to contribute to the reaction, and it remains unclear which of them is predominant.
Lastly, the synthetic application of the diboryl allene products was briefly demonstrated in Scheme 3. The regioselective Suzuki-

Miyaura cross-coupling reactions were conducted successfully using sterically biased substrates such as 18 and 4e. Product 20 could undergo either mono- or di-homologation under precisely tuned conditions,<sup>[21]</sup> followed by oxidation to provide allenyl or homoallenyl alcohols, respectively.

In summary, we have disclosed the first example of accessing 1,3-diboryl allenes from gem-iododiboron compounds in the presence of alkynyl Grignard reagents. The reaction is highly efficient and can accommodate steric hindrance and various functional groups. Mechanistic studies have suggested that the cascade process consists of a formal substitution and a subsequent isomerization. The isotope-labeling crossover experiment indicated that the isomerization proceeds through an unconventional intermolecular boryl group transfer. Utilization of the products was also briefly demonstrated.

In an argon-filled glove box, to a 15 mL vial equipped with a magnetic stir bar was added the iododiboron compound (0.1 mmol, 1.0 equiv.). The vial was sealed with a polypropylene open-top cap with PTFE/silicone septum, then removed from the glove box. Toluene (1.0 mL) was added and the vial was cooled in an ice-cold water bath. Grignard reagent (0.11 mmol, 1.1 equiv.) was slowly added. The mixture was then warmed to room temperature and stirred for 3 h. Upon completion, the reaction was quenched with sat.
\mathsf { N H } _ { 4 } \mathsf { C l }

solution (2 mL) and extracted with Et O (3 x 2 mL). The combined organic layers were dried over Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, filtered, and concentrated in vacuo, and the crude reaction mixture was purified by column chromatography on pre-dried silica gel.
